short: The largest of the imperial fora, funded by the plunder of Dacia and designed by Apollodorus of Damascus.
full:
Trajan's architect Apollodorus of Damascus laid out the largest and last of Rome's imperial fora, begun around 107 CE and inaugurated in 112. Financed by the spoils of the Dacian Wars, which had ended in 106, the complex required cutting away part of the saddle between the Capitoline and Quirinal hills. A vast colonnaded piazza led to the Basilica Ulpia, two libraries, and, behind them, Trajan's Column; a separate multi-storey market building of shops and offices, built into the excavated hillside, has become known as Trajan's Markets.

The forum served as Rome's principal law court and civic meeting ground, its scale meant to signal that no further conquest could add to what Trajan had already achieved. Later emperors used it for ceremonial occasions into the fourth century, and its ruins, excavated from the early twentieth century onward, remain the clearest surviving evidence of how the imperial fora were planned as a connected sequence.
